hints: Start by thinking about where most of the ATP in aerobic respiration actually comes from - it is not mainly from glycolysis or the Krebs cycle itself.
Recall what reduced NAD and reduced FAD do after they are formed, and what they carry to the mitochondria.
Compare the basic chemistry of carbohydrate, lipid and protein - think about proportion of carbon and hydrogen to oxygen in each.
Link the number of C-H bonds in the substrate, especially in fatty acid tails, to the amount of hydrogen that can be removed during oxidation.
Follow the hydrogen: think about what hydrogen splits into and how electrons and protons are used to make ATP.
Finish by linking more hydrogen per unit mass to more proton pumping, more chemiosmosis and a higher ATP yield.
walkthrough:
Where ATP Really Comes From**
In aerobic respiration, only a little ATP is made directly in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle. Most ATP is made at the end, using reduced NAD and reduced FAD to power the electron transport chain and chemiosmosis. So anything that gives you more reduced NAD and FAD will give you more ATP.

Different Fuels Hold Different Amounts of Hydrogen**
Carbohydrates are already partly oxidised - they contain a lot of oxygen relative to carbon and hydrogen, for example $C_6H_{12}O_6$. Lipids, especially the long fatty acid tails, contain very long chains of $C-H$ bonds with little oxygen. Proteins are in between and variable. So per gram, lipids can release far more hydrogen atoms on complete oxidation.

From Hydrogen to Proton Gradient to ATP**
When the substrate is oxidised in glycolysis, link reaction, Krebs cycle and beta-oxidation, the removed hydrogen is used to reduce $NAD$ to $NADH$ and $FAD$ to $FADH_2$. These donate hydrogen to the electron transport chain. Hydrogen splits into protons ($H^+$) and electrons ($e^-$). Electrons pass along carriers, releasing energy to pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Protons then flow back through ATP synthase in chemiosmosis, making ATP by oxidative phosphorylation. More C-H bonds means more NADH / FADH2, a larger proton gradient and more ATP per unit mass, making lipids the most energy-dense substrate.

Final answer: Different substrates contain different numbers of hydrogen atoms / C-H bonds per unit mass; lipids have most hydrogen, in fatty acid tails. Oxidation of substrate releases hydrogen to reduce NAD / FAD. Reduced NAD / FAD donate hydrogen to the electron transport chain, where it dissociates into protons and electrons. Electron energy is used to pump protons to form a proton gradient for chemiosmosis / oxidative phosphorylation. More hydrogen gives more ATP, so lipids have highest relative energy value per unit mass.

hints: Start with what RQ compares - think about the two gases exchanged during aerobic respiration.
Remember RQ is a ratio, so be precise about volume or moles per unit time and which gas is on top.
Think about what apparatus lets you measure gas uptake by a small organism like germinating seeds.
Consider how you could remove one of the gases from the air so that any change in volume is due only to the other gas.
Think about how you would detect that volume change - what moves in a sealed tube.
Recall what conditions must be kept constant so that gas volume changes are only due to respiration.
Plan how to get the second value you need - what would you change to measure total gas exchange as well as oxygen alone.
Think about how to time your readings and what the difference between the two sets of readings tells you.
Finish by linking your two measurements to the calculation of RQ.
walkthrough:
Defining RQ**
$RQ$ tells you what substrate is being respired. It is calculated as: $$RQ = \frac{volume \text{ of } CO_2 \text{ given out}}{volume \text{ of } O_2 \text{ taken in}}$$ measured in the same time period, using volumes or moles. For example carbohydrate gives $RQ$ about 1.0, lipid gives about 0.7.

Measuring Oxygen Uptake Alone**
Place a known mass of germinating barley seeds on mesh in a sealed respirometer tube so they are exposed to air but not touching any chemicals. Add $KOH$ or $NaOH$ solution or soda lime in the tube to absorb all the $CO_2$ given out. Connect to a manometer or capillary tube containing a coloured fluid. Keep temperature and air pressure constant using a water bath and a control tube, because gas volume is very sensitive to these. As oxygen is taken up and $CO_2$ is absorbed, pressure falls and fluid moves. Record distance moved in a set time to calculate rate of oxygen uptake.

Measuring Carbon Dioxide Release to Get RQ**
Now repeat the experiment exactly the same but without the alkali. Both oxygen uptake and $CO_2$ release now affect the manometer reading. The difference between the reading with alkali (oxygen only) and without alkali (net gas exchange) is due to $CO_2$ given out. Measure oxygen uptake after a set time in both tubes, calculate volume of $CO_2$ released, then divide $CO_2$ out by $O_2$ in to get RQ of the germinating seeds.

Final answer: RQ = volume / moles of carbon dioxide given out divided by volume / moles of oxygen taken in per unit time. Using a respirometer: place germinating barley seeds on mesh/gauze in sealed tube with KOH / NaOH / soda lime to absorb $CO_2$; connect to manometer / capillary tube with fluid / syringe. Fall in fluid = oxygen uptake in given time at constant temperature and pressure. Repeat without alkali; difference between readings = $CO_2$ released. Calculate $RQ = CO_2 / O_2$.
